world.setting: A high-rise apartment building in a Black urban neighborhood; action takes place almost entirely inside a descending elevator over sixty seconds.

will.name: Will
will.role: Protagonist; 15-year-old boy riding the elevator down with Shawn's gun, deciding whether to follow the rules and take revenge.
will.look: Black boy, 15, lean and slightly built, short natural hair, wearing a dark charcoal zip-up hoodie over a black t-shirt, dark blue jeans, white sneakers; he carries a gun tucked in his waistband; his expression moves between numbness and fear.

shawn.name: Shawn
shawn.role: Will's older brother, shot dead the day before the story begins; appears as a ghost in the elevator.
shawn.look: Black young man, about 20, average build, short hair, wearing a dark burgundy t-shirt and dark jeans; a ghost presence—calm, sad expression.

mark.name: Uncle Mark
mark.role: Will's uncle and a former artist; appears as a ghost; uses narrative distance to expose the truth about the rules and the family cycle of violence.
mark.look: Black man, about 40, average build, natural hair grown out, wearing an olive-green jacket over a worn grey shirt and dark trousers; thoughtful and slightly weary expression.

buck.name: Buck
buck.role: The man who gave Shawn the gun; appears as a ghost; was a small-time street hustler who ended up dead. He shows Will that the rules are a trap passed hand to hand.
buck.look: Black young man, about 25, stocky build, close-cropped hair, wearing a dark navy blue bomber jacket over a white shirt and black jeans; wary and tired expression.

pop.name: Pop
pop.role: Will's grandfather figure who sought revenge after Uncle Mark was killed; appears as a ghost; tells Will the true story of what revenge actually cost.
pop.look: Black older man, about 60, stocky and worn-down build, greying close-cropped hair and stubble, wearing a brown cardigan over a plaid shirt and dark trousers; sorrowful eyes.

dani.name: Dani
dani.role: A young girl from the neighborhood, killed by a stray bullet; appears as a ghost in the elevator; the youngest voice and the most innocent victim of the rules.
dani.look: Black girl, about 10, small build, natural hair in two puffs, wearing a lavender school dress and white shoes; a ghost with an expression of quiet knowing.

elevator.look: The interior of a steel elevator in a worn apartment building: scuffed metal walls, a floor counter above the doors counting down from 8 to L, dim fluorescent light.

street.look: A city street in a Black urban neighborhood at dusk — cracked sidewalks, brick facades, a corner where the shooting happened.

abstract.look: Whitespace representing the open page of verse — single words suspended, rule lists, the void between beats.

signatureObjects.name: The Gun
signatureObjects.why: The physical gun tucked in Will's waistband is the book's central object — it is the inherited weapon, the choice point, the weight of the rules made literal. No shared icon depicts a gun being inherited as a moral test.

signatureObjects.name: Elevator Floor Counter
signatureObjects.why: The descending floor numbers (8 → L) are the book's clock — each floor is a ghost, a story, a reason to reconsider. The countdown IS the structure of the poem. No shared icon depicts this.

signatureObjects.name: The Three Rules
signatureObjects.why: The rules are shown as a literal numbered list in the poem: 1. Don't cry. 2. Don't snitch. 3. Revenge. This list is the antagonist of the story — a visual card of three lines. No shared icon depicts an inherited code of conduct this specific.

spine.claim: Will, 15, steps into the elevator carrying his dead brother's gun, bound by three rules he did not write: don't cry, don't snitch, seek revenge.
The ghosts of Buck, Shawn, and Dani enter the elevator floor by floor, each one a link in the chain — and each one was following the same rules when they died.
Uncle Mark and Pop reveal the full history: the rules are not protection — they are a cycle that kills everyone who follows them.
Will is forced to see his act of revenge not as justice but as the next link in a chain of inherited grief — and the verdict is not given to him.
The elevator doors open at the lobby. The book ends. Jason Reynolds refuses to tell us what Will does — because the choice belongs to the reader.
